q: Can the Kundrat 2020 fitted coefficients (Tables 1-2) be independently re-derived from a public track-structure code such as Geant4-DNA (Opt2/Opt4 physics list) or TOPAS-nBio, within the paper's quoted <2% RMS envelope (up to ~9% for DSB clusters), thereby providing an existence proof of the underlying yields without needing PARTRAC source access?
basis: PARTRAC itself is closed in-house GSF/HMGU code and the raw simulation-point tables behind Figures 1-5 are not deposited anywhere accessible. Without an independent MC channel, the paper's central validation claim is not falsifiable outside GSF.
next_steps: Set up Geant4-DNA Option 2 with an equivalent chromatin-fibre geometry model (e.g. the OCLA or DBSCAN-style clustering post-processor); run H, He, C, Ne at the same LET grid used by Kundrat; fit Eq.1/Eq.2 to those points; compare coefficient-by-coefficient and report per-ion RMS deviation between the two MC codes. All free/open-source; feasible on m1 or a single Spark GPU node in a few CPU-days.

q: How do the analytical formulas extrapolate to non-standard track structures beyond the fitted set, in particular heavy ions past Ne (e.g. Ar, Fe at deep-space or hadron-therapy energies) and low-energy secondary electrons (sub-keV) where track-end effects dominate?
basis: The paper explicitly warns against extrapolation outside the fitted LET and ion ranges, and our own analysis surfaced a concrete failure mode: the H-proton DSB-site row lacks the overkill denominator (p4,p5 = N.A.) and therefore diverges unbounded past its fitted range, contradicting the paper's ~15 sites/Gy/Gbp peak claim.
next_steps: (1) Enumerate the exact fitted LET domain per ion from Table 1-2 supplementary metadata and code it as hard clamps in formulas.py; (2) generate fresh Geant4-DNA points for Ar and Fe at 1-500 keV/um and see whether Eq.1/Eq.2 with re-fitted coefficients still describe the yield curves; (3) probe sub-keV secondary-electron regime with the low-energy TOPAS-nBio electromagnetic physics list; (4) publish a fit-domain map alongside any redistribution of the formulas.

q: Can these analytical yield formulas be integrated with modern chromatin-geometry models (fractal globule, whole-nucleus Hi-C-derived geometry, phase-separated compartments) to produce spatially-resolved DSB-cluster predictions, or are the fits inherently tied to the PARTRAC-era chromatin-fibre representation?
basis: The paper's DSB-site classification depends on the underlying chromatin model used inside PARTRAC (a 30 nm solenoid / fibre representation of roughly 2000 Mbp of DNA). Modern data-driven chromatin models produce very different local-density distributions, which would change DSB-clustering statistics for the same track structure.
next_steps: Replace the implicit uniform-fibre geometry with an explicit voxelized chromatin density map derived from Micro-C or 3D-genome models; recompute DSB-site clustering (using e.g. DBSCAN with a 25 bp threshold as in the Kundrat convention) on the same MC track set; report the sensitivity of the DSB-site yield to the chromatin-geometry choice. This is a paper-scale investigation but each individual step is free.

q: Do the fitted formulas remain quantitatively accurate at ultra-high dose rates such as FLASH (>=40 Gy/s), where inter-track chemistry and radical recombination begin to matter, or do they systematically over-predict DSB yields because they were fit at conventional dose rates where inter-track effects are negligible?
basis: Kundrat's PARTRAC runs behind Tables 1-2 were done in the single-track / low-dose-rate regime where damage yields are linear in dose. FLASH radiotherapy operates in a regime where oxygen depletion, radical-radical recombination and inter-track interactions are hypothesized to reduce net damage, none of which is represented in Eq.1/Eq.2.
next_steps: Compare Eq.1/Eq.2 predictions against published FLASH-regime yield measurements (e.g. Adrian et al. 2020, Wilson et al. 2020) or against dose-rate-aware MC codes (TRAX-CHEM, GEANT4-DNA-Chem) run at 0.03 Gy/s vs 100 Gy/s. Report the ratio Y_FLASH/Y_conv predicted by the analytical formulas (should be ~1 by construction) vs measured/simulated (expected < 1). Free; endpoint-only literature comparison plus one open-source MC campaign.

q: How sensitive is the paper's headline <2% RMS fit quality to the specific choice of functional forms in Eqs. 1-2, and could an ML-driven symbolic-regression pipeline (e.g. PySR, AI-Feynman) discover more parsimonious or more physically-motivated analytical surrogates for other track-structure MC codes (Geant4-DNA, TOPAS-nBio, KURBUC)?
basis: Eqs. 1-2 have the flavour of hand-crafted phenomenological forms; there is no a-priori argument that log-squared damping (Eq.1) or power-law-over-power-law (Eq.2) is the uniquely correct compression of the underlying MC. A different functional form could match the data equally well or better and might extrapolate more safely.
next_steps: (1) Generate a modest yield grid (H/He/C/Ne at 10-20 LET points) with an open MC code; (2) run PySR with a physics-friendly operator set on that grid and report the top-k discovered expressions with their RMS deviation and parameter count; (3) score against Eqs. 1-2 on both in-range fit quality and out-of-range behaviour; (4) report whether the discovered forms admit interpretable radiobiological meaning. All free/open-source; ~1 GPU-day per ion on a Spark node.
